Besides the act of prayer itself, love is for me the most perplexing part of Christianity.

Perhaps there is an objective state corresponding with love, such that we could study a PET scan of the brain while someone is in the religious mode and find that, yes, this person loves the God with whom they are speaking. They point me to things like, "God's chasing you. He wants you. He wants to find you. You mean everything to Him."

Those things always felt really wonderful to hear, but it always struck me how embodied the verbs felt.

The entire approach wants to make gratitude a huge component of love, and that's just doesn't sit right with me. It's inevitable that you encounter distinctions about kinds of love. What are they...Eros, Philia, Storge and Agape. You have erotic and romantic love, love of my friends and siblings/parents, love for one's children, and love that mirrors God's love for man.

The appeal to agape love by most Christians still appeals to phenomenology, and they attempt to cause you to adopt a God perspective, imagining what it would take to "give the only begotten son" (I must project these internal states onto the Father, as though the infinite being reduces to a love between parent and child). This, by the way, is precisely where the things we were discussing about the trinity become important: this appeal only works if Christ is, in fact, the Father's Son. It's confused by the fact that the Christ and the Father are supposed to be hypostases of the same divine being. On that account, it becomes something more akin to self-sacrifice, returning us back to notions of gratitude.

Something like some crazed Roman emperor that could sleep as well leaving world destruction up to a coin flip. He petitions a man for a game. He tells the man: "You will decide whether humanity is destroyed today. Choose to push one of the two red buttons, or give up your life. One of the two red buttons activates every nuclear device on earth to explode. The other does nothing. There are 50/50 odds you destroy the world. Alternatively, you can allow me to kill you and humanity will be surely be spared."

The poor Chinese man, unwilling to take a chance on killing other people, decides to give up his life, saving the world.

I could not love him. I could be monumentally gracious, and incredibly moved emotionally, hell, even spiritually I guess. But I could not love him. It seems that love only enters the picture once he is able to become a symbol, an archetype for all goodness, the better parts of us all, a father and a savior in spirit. Perhaps over time with enough legendary attachments, that's what this man becomes.

As it concerns the experience of loving God, I just don't see that this is possible without attaching very vague yet powerful archetypes of parental figures to a concept. It's as if a necessary aspect of maturing in the human lifecycle involves coming to understand your biological parents as humans (dissolving their godlike archetypal power over your psyche), and so we replace them in that latter respect, or externalize that function into the ether - one possible reason why God is so anthropomorphized.

It's everything our real parents could not be, which is perhaps also why God's dual nature allows it to be comforter and vindicator in any way that serves our interests (just like parents would be likely to): wrathful devastator when we need to defeat an enemy, while simultaneously a being concerned with everyday conversation with me before bed. It's the spectrum of parental power (phenomenologically) from the tucker-inner, to the look of disappointment that could destroy your world.

Maybe this is also why in our religious systems we cannot but help to understand God as a set of prototypes that fully reduce this complexity to basic constituents: father, son, spirit (love), mother (Mary), angels (delocalizes wrath from the parent), and the devil (demonizes the object of father's wrath). On the whole it all seems like a complex for maintaining our dual phenomenology of parents, maintaining the pristine nature of love and wrath separately, so that we never have to unite the two in our single object of love: mom or dad.
